newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN BROADCASTING CORP MIDDAY UPDATE.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN BROADCASTING CORP MIDDAY UPDATE.

text.p: ALSTON PLANS PROTECTION FOR INTERNET TRADERS
The Federal Government has proposed setting up a national registration authority to protect people doing business on the Internet.
The move was announced by the Communications Minister, RichardAlston, at an Internet conference in Sydney today.
Senator Alston said online commerce was about to explode both globally and within Australia.
By 2002, it was expected that 30 per cent of retail transactions, comprising 22 per cent of revenue, would be conducted on the Internet.
To protect customers and businesses from legal problems in electronic transactions, Senator Alston has called for a national registration authority to check the bona fides of digital signatures.
ECONOMIC GROWTH OVERDUE, SAYS INDUSTRY GROUP
Strong economic growth is achievable and overdue, according to the Australian Chamber of Manufactures.
Chamber chief executive Allan Handberg was reacting to a speech by Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane, who said the economy could grow by 4.5 per cent or more in the next few years.
Mr Handberg said he also agreed with Mr Macfarlane's comments that Australians will have to work longer and harder.
"Most Australians are gradually coming to recognise that we are slipping backwards," Mr Handberg said.
PARENTS WANT APOLOGY FROM VANSTONE
A parents' group has complained to Prime Minister John Howard about Education Minister Amanda Vanstone's comments linking unemployment with the quality of public education.
Following the announcement of rising unemployment figures, Senator Vanstone said students educated in the public system were 10 times more likely to end up unemployed.
The president of the Federation of P & C Associations of New South Wales, Ros Brennan, said Senator Vanstone should apologise for her comments.
She said it had to be made plain to Senator Vanstone that public education should not be belittled.
BASKETBALLERS SLAM-DUNK DRUGS MESSAGE
Some of Australia's top basketballers have signed up to take part in an anti-drugs program for children aged 7 to 12.
In a national first, Operation Smart Start aims to involve Victorian children in sport to keep them away from drugs.
Inspired by a successful project in Chicago helping ghetto kids off the street, Operation Smart Start will involve 45 Victorian schools and about 12,000 children.
The program involves a day-long basketball clinic and an anti-drug motivational talk by a celebrity basketballer.
Australian team star Andrew Gaze, who will take part in the program, said it was a great way for children to improve their self-esteem through sport and stay away from drugs.
